senses: Tending to ramble, to wander aimlessly or to make meandering digressions.
examples: Is your writing wordy and rambly? Try these two new products and you may discover that you can be a better, faster writer than you think!
Boris Johnson's speech to the nation on Sunday May 10 was rambly, incoherent, and he failed dismally in his attempt to sound Churchillian.

senses: One who, or that which, hulls; especially, an agricultural machine for removing the hulls from grain; a hulling machine.
A person or thing that ascends.
The portion of a lowercase letter that extends above the midline.
A lowercase letter that has such a portion, such as d or h.
A lava field in Mexico or the Western US.
ety: From Spanish pedregal (“a stony place”), from piedra (“stone”).

senses: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 20.8 cm.
A traditional Portuguese unit of length, usually equivalent to about 22 cm.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish palmo (“handspan”) and Portuguese palmo (“handspan”), both from Latin palmus. Doublet of palm, palma, and pam.

senses: The female equivalent of a batboy.
A person who operates railway switches that route trains onto rail tracks.
A person whose job is to help in the switching of railcars in a railway yard.
examples: This route is repeated automatically on the control panel of the appropriate box as flashing indications covering the track circuits involved and the switchman obeys the instruction by setting up the required route.

senses: A soldier enlisted in an artillery unit or who uses artillery.
A sudden or unsteady movement.
ety: Originally a nautical term, found in lee-larches (“the sudden and violent rolls of a ship to the leeward in high seas”), of unknown origin. Possibly the same as lurch (“to move stealthily, evade by stooping”) (see below), or from French lâcher (“to let go”).

senses: Any of group of nine public-sector undertakings in India.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi नवरत्न (navratna), from Sanskrit नवरत्न (navaratna).

senses: Sweets; confectionery.
Synonym of spelt.
examples: Spelt or dinkel is an ancient form of wheat. Dinkel flour is marketed in several grades (kernels, white, whole-grain, etc.). It has a strong flavour and makes very good bread.

senses: To make secular.
A unit of measure of the power of a lens or mirror, equal to the reciprocal of its focal length in meters. Myopia is diagnosed and measured in diopters.
The dioptre adjustment mechanism of a pair of binoculars or of a camera viewfinder.
A lens element attached to the front of a photographic lens to shorten the lens's minimum focus distance; also called a "close-up filter".
ety: From Latin dioptra, from Ancient Greek διόπτρα (dióptra).

senses: Shaped like a sword, ensiform.
The decomposition of any material by microorganisms.
The study of the elderly, and of the aging process itself.
A method of betting in which the bettor, in order to win, must pick the first four finishers of a race in the correct sequence.
A foul-smelling plant grown in Asia, Amorphophallus konjac.
ety: From the Latinized binomial name for the plant, Amorphophallus konjac or Arisaema konjac in earlier texts, from Japanese 蒟蒻, 菎蒻 (konnyaku) or Korean 곤약 (gonyak). The Japanese term probably derives from Old Japanese, in turn from Middle Chinese 蒟蒻 (MC kjuX|kjuH nyak). The plant is not native to the Japanese archipelago, and was imported from China.

senses: The highest voice or part, often a violin or soprano vocal line.
A person who walks about in their sleep; a sleepwalker.
ety: Borrowed from French somnambuliste, from Medieval Latin somnambulus (“sleepwalker”). By surface analysis, somn- + -ambulist.
examples: The clergyman floundered a moment, as is usual with an absent man who is recovering the train of his ideas, or a somnambulist when he is suddenly awakened.

The slim one got up and walked straight at me - still knitting with downcast eyes - and only just as I began to think of getting out of her way, as you would for a somnambulist, stood still, and looked up.

senses: The extent to which something can easily be sold
examples: Although even the most outrageous outfits would go on sale the next day, the salability of a "medieval biker dress" or "paper bag shorts" seemed a secondary consideration.

senses: That leads to immunomodulation
A flaky pastry (typically filled with either mung bean, pork bits, purple yam, azuki bean, or etc.)
ety: Borrowed from Tagalog hopia, from Spanish hopia, from Hokkien, possibly 好餅 /好饼 (hó piáⁿ, literally “good pastry”) according to Chan-Yap (1980) and Manuel (1948). See also Early Manila Hokkien 香餅 /香饼 (hioⁿ-piáⁿ, literally “fragrant pastry”), Indonesian bakpia. Compare Cebuano hopya.

senses: Namely, to wit, that is to say (used when clarifying or naming the preceding item or topic)
ety: Borrowed from Latin vidēlicet, which itself is a contraction of vidēre licet, meaning "it is permitted to see".

senses: concurrence of the position or influence of stars
similarity of condition, fortune, etc., as prefigured by astrological calculation
ety: From Ancient Greek συναστρία (sunastría, “conjunction of the stars”).

senses: Catering to tourists; touristy.
Typical of tourists.
ety: From tourist + -ic, popularized by its similarity to Romance words like French touristique and Spanish turístico.

senses: A female shepherd.
A large and deep armchair with a cushion.
ety: From Middle English scheperdesse, shepperdesse; equivalent to shepherd + -ess.
examples: September 2014, New York Film Festival to Revive Paul Grimault’s Animated Classic IndieWire the satirical The King And The Mockingbird follows a chimney sweep and shepherdess on the run from a tyrannical king

senses: The use of property, or an existing mortgage, as security for a loan, etc.
A tax levied for a specific expenditure.
ety: From hypothecate + -ion. From Latin hypothecatio, from hypotheco (“to pledge as collateral”), from Greek.
examples: It is, however, precisely here that the weakness of hypothecation lies, for governments are not likely readily to surrender control over the disposition of taxes they impose.
Either way, effectively the government is simply using the hypothecated tax as part of general revenue, and the hypothecation is a sham.

Local authorities have linked the scheme to broader climate ambitions. Indeed, some of the funding for the stations has come from hypothecation of monies received through Birmingham's Clean Air Zone charges.

senses: The wood of these trees.
The bark of these trees, formerly used in treating fever.
A tannin extracted from these trees.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish quebracho, from quebrar (“to break”) + hacha (“axe”).

senses: food, a meal
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani کھانا (khānā) / खाना (khānā), from Sanskrit खादन (khādana), from खाद् (khād, “to eat”, root) + -अन (-ana), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kʰād-, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷh₂ed-.

senses: A member of a local African military or police unit, usually one serving in a European colonial force.
ety: From Swahili askari (“soldier”), from Arabic عَسْكَرِيّ (ʕaskariyy). Doublet of lascar.

senses: Any of several slow changes in an astronomical body's rotational or orbital parameters.
ety: From Middle English precessioun, precession, from Medieval Latin prēcessiōn-, prēcessio, from Latin praecēdō.

senses: The bar on a plough which projects downward beneath the beam to connect to the sole.
ety: Inherited from Middle English schethe; possibly related to or even etymologically identical to sheath. Compare Old English sċēaþa, Middle Dutch schêde (“nail”).

senses: A new feature, a novelty.
A person who or a thing which beautifies or makes beautiful.
examples: The sea is no beautifier, certainly; sailors do grow old betimes; I have often observed it; they soon lose the look of youth.
Meg had spent the time in working as well as waiting, growing womanly in character, wise in housewifery arts, and prettier than ever; for love is a great beautifier.

senses: A hammerer; a forgeman.
The quality of making rash or arbitrary decisions, especially in an impulsive or forceful manner.
The condition or quality of being impetuous, impatient; fury; violence.
ety: From English impetuous + -ity, from Middle French impétuosité, from Old French.
examples: Again his lordship began his long and deliberate perusal, while Henrietta watched the slow motion of his eyes with a degree of impetuosity she could scarcely repress.

senses: To fly over something.
To fly too far past something.
examples: My family planned to take pictures from the ground as I overflew them in the hot air balloon.
In the canopy, friendly birds (not the desperate, demented scavengers that sometimes overflew the plains) chirped and laboured on their nests.
The small size of the airstrip meant that pilots would frequently overfly and have to circle back.

senses: The production of a coating of myelin around an axon
